import FormalConjecturesUtil
import FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«20»

/-!
# Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture

This file is a Wikipedia-facing entry point for the formalization in
`FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«20»`.

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower_(mathematics))
-/

reformulations.difference: This theorem is imported, not declared in the reviewed file. Its helper uses exactly n-element sets and the inclusive forcing threshold |F| ≥ f(n,k), whereas Wikipedia initially uses sets of size at most n and a strict forcing threshold. Lean also uses a strict exponential bound with natural-number constants and includes the trivial petal counts.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Wikipedia explicitly recognizes both uniformization by dummy elements and the alternative threshold Sun(n,k)=f_Wikipedia(n,k)+1. Adding private dummy elements preserves intersections between distinct sets, so bounded-size and uniform families give the same forcing problem. For positive n, increasing the exponential base to an integer greater than C+1 absorbs the threshold shift and changes a non-strict exponential bound into the strict Lean bound; the converse follows immediately. Petal counts 0, 1, and 2 are trivial, and the source's zero-size case is automatic. These differences therefore do not change the conjecture.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower_(mathematics) — revision 1372848827; definitions, threshold conventions, sunflower lemma, Erdős–Rado conjecture, and weak conjecture.
review.notes: The reviewed 27-line file contains only imports and a module docstring: it introduces no mathematical declarations, answer slots, or status attributes. It correctly serves as an entry point to the cited conjecture. Wikipedia still records the strong Erdős–Rado conjecture as open; its solved weak conjecture is a different problem. Scratch Lean checks confirmed the imported definitions, positivity-based finiteness safeguards, empty/singleton sunflower cases, and f(n,0)=0 and f(n,1)=1. The supplementary Erdős Problems URL returned a Cloudflare challenge, but the file's directly cited Wikipedia source was accessible and sufficient.
